content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the east is most commonly understood as the direction associated with God's presence, glory, and salvation — the direction of the rising sun (dawn/light), of Eden, and of the expected coming (and return) of Christ. This underlies the historic Christian practice of praying and orienting churches toward the east.", "primary_basis": ["Genesis 2:8 (God plants the garden 'in the east, in Eden')", "Ezekiel 43:1-4 (the glory of God enters the temple from the east; cf. Ezekiel 10:18-19 and 11:23, where the glory departs eastward)", "Ezekiel 44:1-2 (the east gate reserved for the LORD)", "Matthew 2:1-2, 9 (the magi come from the east, having seen his star in the east/at its rising)", "Matthew 24:27 (as lightning comes from the east... so will be the coming of the Son of Man)", "Malachi 4:2 ('sun of righteousness' rising, read messianically)", "Luke 1:78 ('the dayspring/sunrise from on high,' anatole, applied to Christ)", "Zechariah 14:4 (the LORD's feet on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem)", "Psalm 103:12 ('as far as the east is from the west,' used for the removal of sin)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Eastward movement as departure, exile, or alienation from God's presence — a literary pattern in Genesis where sin drives people east (Adam and Eve, Cain, Babel, Lot), with return toward God pictured as movement back west toward Eden/the sanctuary.", "basis": ["Genesis 3:24 (cherubim placed at the east of Eden after expulsion)", "Genesis 4:16 (Cain dwells east of Eden, in Nod)", "Genesis 11:2 (migration eastward to Shinar/Babel)", "Genesis 13:11 (Lot journeys east toward Sodom)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The east as the source of judgment or destructive power, especially via the 'east wind' (a scorching desert wind) and invading empires (Assyria, Babylon) coming from the east.", "basis": ["Genesis 41:6, 23, 27 (grain blasted by the east wind in Pharaoh's dream)", "Exodus 10:13 and 14:21 (east wind brings the locusts and parts the sea)", "Hosea 13:15; Jeremiah 18:17; Jonah 4:8 (east wind as instrument of judgment or affliction)", "Isaiah 41:2 (one stirred up from the east, read of Cyrus)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The east ('people of the east,' bene qedem) as the realm of foreign nations, pagan wisdom, and Israel's enemies (Midianites, Amalekites, diviners from the east), sometimes read symbolically as worldly or occult wisdom contrasted with divine revelation.", "basis": ["Judges 6:3, 33 (Midianites and people of the east raid Israel)", "1 Kings 4:30 (Solomon's wisdom exceeds the wisdom of all the people of the east)", "Isaiah 2:6 (the house of Jacob filled with influences 'from the east,' diviners)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "The east as simply an idiom for great or immeasurable distance rather than a theological direction, especially in the sin-removal text.", "basis": ["Psalm 103:12 ('as far as the east is from the west')"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Warning against sun/east-facing worship as idolatry, showing that eastward orientation itself is not inherently holy.", "basis": ["Ezekiel 8:16 (men in the temple with their backs to the sanctuary, worshiping the sun toward the east)"], "prominence": "rare"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "medium", "notes": "The east carries a recognized dual valence in scripture and in Christian interpretation. The positive strand — dawn, Eden, the glory of God returning from the east, and the eschatological coming of Christ — is the most prominent in Christian liturgical tradition (ad orientem prayer and church orientation, attested from the patristic era, e.g., Origen, Basil, John of Damascus). The negative strand (eastward exile in Genesis; east wind judgment; enemies from the east) is well established in academic biblical studies as a literary motif but functions alongside, not against, the dominant liturgical-theological reading. Because the symbolism is genuinely two-sided and context-dependent, the consensus is settled only in the sense that the Christ-oriented, God's-presence reading is clearly the dominant symbolic assignment in Christian teaching; confidence is rated medium rather than high because the term has multiple materially different, well-attested strands rather than one exclusive meaning."}
